title: Judaism: Shabbat candles
hookLine: on Friday at dusk, two candles are lit and rest begins

cards: Friday, late afternoon. The inbox still open, the groceries half put away, the phone buzzing with plans. At the same hour, in a Jewish home, a kitchen table is set.

Someone strikes a match and lights two candles. She draws her hands around the flames three times, covers her eyes, and says a blessing. When she uncovers them, nothing in the room has moved, and yet the week is over.

teach.b: Shabbat means rest, or ceasing. It runs from just before sunset on Friday until nightfall on Saturday. Why two candles?
A common answer: the Ten Commandments appear twice in the Torah.

In Exodus the commandment begins, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society words, "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy it begins with a different verb: observe it, or guard it. Remember, and keep.
One candle for each. In many homes the woman of the house lights them, though anyone may, and a little before sunset, so no one lights a fire once Shabbat has begun. That's why the eyes are covered.
A blessing usually comes before the act, but here the blessing is what begins the rest, so you light, hide the flames, bless, and then look.

The big idea: for six days, the Torah says, God made the world, and on the seventh God rested. Shabbat invites people to copy that rhythm. No work, no buying and selling, in many homes no phones or driving.
Observance varies widely: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and secular Jews keep it in very different ways.
The twentieth-century teacher Abraham Joshua Heschel called Shabbat a palace in time: most holy places are buildings, but this one is built out of hours.
And an old saying from the writer Ahad Ha'am turns it around: more than the Jews have kept Shabbat, Shabbat has kept the Jews.

how: In many Jewish homes, two candles are lit shortly before sunset on Friday with a blessing, the eyes covered, and Shabbat is kept until nightfall on Saturday; how strictly varies from family to family.

practice: Picture two flames in front of you, or look at any light nearby. Name one thing from this week you're putting down, just for these two minutes, a worry, a task, a screen, and then one thing you want to remember.
